sections.section_title: Case Presentation and Initial Diagnostic Workup
sections.description: This section presents the patient's clinical presentation, physical examination findings, and the initial laboratory and imaging investigations that revealed multisystem involvement. It covers the hematologic, hepatic, pulmonary, musculoskeletal, and neurologic findings, as well as the identification of severe nutritional deficiencies, establishing the foundation for understanding why a broader diagnostic workup was pursued.
subtopics: Patient demographics and presenting symptoms: 5-year history of progressive fatigue, weakness, exertional dyspnoea, and weight loss
Physical examination findings: pallor, icterus, premature greying, knuckle hyperpigmentation, bald tongue, thoracic scoliosis, thenar atrophy, hepatosplenomegaly, and reduced breath sounds
Initial hematologic evaluation: pancytopenia, low reticulocyte count, dimorphic anaemia, basophilic stippling, Cabot rings, and hypersegmented neutrophils
Bone marrow examination: trilineage haematopoiesis with erythroid hyperplasia and increased iron stores without malignancy or dysplasia
Nutritional deficiency identification: severe vitamin B12 and folate deficiency with elevated iron and ferritin consistent with ineffective erythropoiesis
Hepatic evaluation: hepatosplenomegaly on ultrasound, transient elastography showing grade II steatosis and cirrhosis, negative autoimmune and infectious workup
Pulmonary and systemic imaging: PET-CT findings of ground-glass haziness, fibrotic changes, inhomogeneous bone marrow uptake, and absence of malignancy
Additional systemic findings: secondary hyperparathyroidism, osteoporosis, and asymmetric sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy on electromyography

sections.description: This section explains the clinical reasoning process that led clinicians from the initial findings to the suspicion of a genetic disorder. It covers why nutritional deficiency alone was insufficient to explain the presentation, how autoimmune and infectious causes were excluded, and how the unique constellation of premature ageing features, persistent cytopenia, and multi-organ fibrosis shifted the diagnostic approach toward a telomere biology disorder.
subtopics: Nutritional deficiency as an initial explanation: severe B12 deficiency accounting for cytopenia and neurological findings, but disproportionate systemic dysfunction after correction
Ineffective erythropoiesis versus haemolysis: low reticulocyte response and marrow findings despite positive DAT, arguing against immune-mediated destruction
Evaluation of hepatic fibrosis aetiology: exclusion of autoimmune hepatitis, viral hepatitis, HIV, CMV, and scrub typhus; only EBV IgG positive
Gastrointestinal evaluation: normal endoscopy with mild chronic gastritis and reduced parietal cells insufficient to explain severity
The diagnostic turning point: recognising the constellation of premature greying, osteoporosis, cytopenia, hepatic fibrosis, and pulmonary fibrosis as a syndromic presentation
Absence of family history and consideration of de novo mutation as a possibility
Hypothesis of a telomere biology disorder: mimicking acquired conditions with variable penetrance and absence of classical mucocutaneous triad of dyskeratosis congenita

sections.section_title: Telomere Biology Disorders and the PARN Gene: Pathophysiology and Genetics
sections.description: This section provides the essential background on telomere biology, the spectrum of telomere biology disorders, and the specific role of the PARN gene. It explains how telomere dysfunction leads to the clinical manifestations observed in this case, the differences between biallelic and monoallelic PARN variants, and why this patient's phenotype fits within the expanding spectrum of PARN-associated disease.
subtopics: Telomere structure and function: repetitive DNA sequences, telomerase complex (TERT and TERC), and the role of telomere maintenance in genomic integrity
Pathophysiology of telomere biology disorders: accelerated telomere attrition leading to cellular senescence in actively dividing tissues
Spectrum of TBDs: dyskeratosis congenita as the prototype, Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome, Revesz syndrome, and Coats plus syndrome
Classical DC triad (oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, reticular skin pigmentation) versus atypical adult presentations without mucocutaneous features
PARN gene function: exoribonuclease role in mRNA deadenylation and TERC 3-prime-end maturation
Haploinsufficiency of PARN: low tolerance to disruptive variants and its essential role in gene regulation
Biallelic PARN variants causing DKCB6 and Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome versus monoallelic variants causing PFBMFT4
Expanding clinical spectrum of PARN mutations: IPF, bone marrow failure, and emerging recognition of hepatic fibrosis
Variable penetrance, somatic genetic rescue, and environmental factors influencing organ-specific manifestations

sections.description: This section details the genetic testing process, the specific PARN variant identified, and the framework used to classify and interpret the variant. It explains the ACMG/AMP classification criteria applied, the concept of a Variant of Uncertain Significance, and how clinical-genetic correlation ultimately supported the diagnosis of a telomere biology disorder despite the variant's uncertain pathogenicity.
subtopics: Clinical exome sequencing as the diagnostic tool and identification of the monoallelic PARN missense variant c.613T>C (p.Cys205Arg)
Location and functional significance of the variant: highly conserved residue within the R3H domain (residues 178–245)
In silico prediction tools: deleterious predictions from LRT, Mutation Assessor, MutationTaster, and SIFT

ACMG/AMP classification criteria applied: PM1 (critical functional domain), PM2 (absent in population databases), PP3 (computational prediction of damaging effect), and PP2 (low rate of benign missense variation in PARN)
Variant of Uncertain Significance: definition, limitations, and the challenge of clinical interpretation
Comparison with other PARN missense variants reported as likely pathogenic in ClinVar: p.Lys59Arg and p.Ala383Val
Clinical-genetic correlation: how the patient's phenotype consistent with TBD spectrum supported diagnostic significance despite VUS classification
Diagnostic gold standards for TBD: next-generation sequencing and flow cytometry-based FISH for telomere length measurement

sections.description: This section covers the treatment approach, the patient's clinical outcome, and the broader clinical lessons from this case. It discusses the supportive management strategy, genetic counselling, surveillance planning, and the important implications for recognising telomere biology disorders in young adults with unexplained multisystem disease, even in the absence of classical features.
subtopics: Treatment of severe B12 deficiency: intravenous cyanocobalamin regimen and folate supplementation
Supportive care: whole blood transfusions, vitamin D and calcium supplementation for osteoporosis, electrolyte correction, and physiotherapy
Genetic counselling for the patient and family following TBD diagnosis
Short-term outcome: symptomatic improvement, stable blood counts, and no new clinical concerns at 2-week follow-up
Long-term surveillance strategy: monitoring hepatic function, pulmonary function, and bone marrow progression
Potential future therapeutic considerations: haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for progressive marrow failure and investigational telomere elongation with androgens (danazol, nandrolone)
Clinical lesson: importance of considering TBDs in young adults with unexplained multisystem disease
Clinical lesson: TBDs can present without the classical mucocutaneous triad of dyskeratosis congenita
Clinical lesson: monoallelic PARN mutations may present with a broader phenotype than IPF alone, including hepatic fibrosis and cytopenia
Clinical lesson: telomere biology disorders may render bone marrow more susceptible to haematopoietic stress, such as nutritional deficiency
